intro: Thirteen verses from the Asaph collection, and a battle poem with no battle in it. The fighting is over before the first line, and all that is reported is the wreckage: broken arrows, a shield, a sword, soldiers asleep who cannot find their own hands. No enemy is named, no year, no king, and Israel does nothing. Two things are worth watching. The verbs run in the past until verse 5, where the psalm turns and speaks to God directly for the rest of the poem. And the four-letter name appears exactly once, in verse 12; everywhere else the psalm says God, which is the signature of the collection it belongs to.

stichs.en: For the leader, with stringed music.
A psalm of Asaph, a song.

verses.summary: Four labels stacked on one piece: choirmaster, strings, psalm, song. The Asaph group tends to pile up its headings this way.

stichs.en: God is known in Judah,
His name is great in Israel.

verses.summary: The claim is geographical before it is theological. God is known in a named place, and what is called great is the name rather than the power.

stichs.en: His shelter came to be in Salem,
and His dwelling in Zion.

verses.summary: Salem and Zion in parallel, one place under two names. Both nouns are modest words, a booth and a lair, used for a permanent presence.

stichs.en: There He broke the fiery arrows of the bow,
shield and sword and war itself. Selah.

verses.summary: The victory is reported only through equipment. The list ends with war, as though war were an object in the same class as a shield and could be snapped alongside it.

stichs.en: You are radiant, You are mighty,
more than the mountains of prey.

verses.summary: The psalm turns to second person here for the first time, and the comparison it makes is one of the least secure phrases in the whole poem.

stichs.en: The stout of heart were stripped bare, they slept their sleep,
and none of the men of valour could find their hands.

verses.summary: The enemy is not killed here, it is disarmed and put to sleep. Warriors who cannot find their hands describes paralysis, not death.

stichs.en: At Your rebuke, God of Jacob,
chariot and horse were stunned into sleep.

verses.summary: The cause is finally named, and it is a rebuke, a word rather than a blow. Chariot and horse go down together with the men who drove them.

stichs.en: You, You are fearsome,
and who can stand before You once Your anger is up?

verses.summary: The pronoun is repeated for weight, and the question that follows gets no answer in the psalm because it is not expecting one.

stichs.en: From heaven You made judgement heard,
the earth was afraid and grew still,

verses.summary: Judgement is issued from heaven and received on earth as silence. Fear and stillness here are one reaction described twice.

stichs.en: when God rose for judgement,
to save all the lowly of the earth. Selah.

verses.summary: The purpose clause shows whose side the judgement was on, and it is not a nation. What is being rescued is a class of people, the lowly.

stichs.en: Surely the wrath of man will praise You;
the remnant of furies You gird on.

verses.summary: The theological hinge, and a hard verse. Human rage ends up producing the praise it set out to prevent, and what is left over is put on like a belt.

stichs.en: Make vows and keep them to the LORD your God;
let all around Him bring tribute to the One who is feared.

glosses: to the One to be feared
verses.summary: The only commands in the psalm, and the only appearance of the four-letter name. What is asked for is vows kept and tribute carried, not applause.

stichs.en: He cuts down the spirit of rulers,
fearsome to the kings of the earth.

verses.summary: The last word is about rulers rather than armies. What gets cut down is spirit, which is where the psalm has been aiming since the sleeping warriors.

pardes.body: The psalm has two tenses and a hinge between them. Verses 2 to 4 are past: God became known, His shelter came to be, He broke the weapons. Verse 5 turns to direct address, and everything after it is present and general. Nothing in the poem names the enemy, the year or the king. The battle survives only in its debris, broken arrows and soldiers who cannot find their hands, and no Israelite is reported doing anything at all. Verse 12 is the single place the four-letter name appears, {{12.2}}; everywhere else the psalm says God, which is the mark of the collection it sits inside.

Three phrases here resist confident translation. At {{5.3}} the words read mountains of prey, and the prefix can be comparative, more majestic than the mountains of prey, or spatial, from the mountains of prey. There is no close parallel to settle it and the reading is disputed. The verb at {{6.0}} is a rare form, taken by some as stripped bare and by others as stupefied. And {{11.4}}, the remnant of furies, leaves it open whether God girds Himself with what is left of human rage or ties it up out of the way. One quieter detail lights the first crux: the noun for dwelling at {{3.3}} is elsewhere the word for a lion's den, so a psalm with a lair in Zion and mountains of prey may be running one image twice.

A reader looking for the event behind the debris reaches for 2 Kings 19 and Isaiah 37, where the Assyrian army encamped against Jerusalem is struck in the night and found in the morning without a battle having been fought. Verses 6 and 7 fit that scene closely: sleep, paralysis, chariot and horse, and no human action on the defending side anywhere in the psalm. The identification is inference, not something the text states, and the psalm keeps the enemy anonymous on purpose. Verse 11 has been read on its own as a principle about history rather than about one night: rage that intends the opposite ends up producing praise, which turns the fury of nations into an instrument instead of an obstacle.

The place is named twice, Salem at {{3.1}} and then Zion, and the first of the two is heard in the tradition as the word for whole and as the root of peace. Read that way the geography carries the argument: the weapons stop working at the place whose name means completeness, and what breaks them is not a counter-army but a rebuke, a word issued from heaven and received on earth as silence. The remnant of wrath in verse 11 belongs to the same reading, a measure held back rather than spent, since a judgement whose stated purpose is to save the lowly has to stop somewhere short of everyone.
